title: multi-gpu-serving-design-nccl-sharding
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures design notes and draft specs for multi-GPU serving in the Redwood inference runtime. Focus areas: tensor & pipeline parallelism choices, NCCL tuning and communication topology, model sharding strategies, and KV-cache consistency and placement. This is a working design (notes, open questions, experiments to run) toward a v0.2 multi-GPU serving feature set for Dedicated and Private deployments.

Scope and goals:
- Support serving large transformer models across multiple GPUs with predictable latency and throughput.
- Provide flexible sharding options: tensor-parallel, pipeline-parallel, and hybrid.
- Minimize per-request tail latency for chat-style workloads while achieving high throughput for batch/streaming workloads.
- Make communication efficient and robust across cloud instances and on-prem hardware (intra-node NVLink and inter-node NICs).
- Ensure KV-cache semantics are correct and performant for pinned sessions and shared session pools.

Assumptions:
- Typical target hardware: A100/H100 nodes with NVLink, and multi-node clusters connected with 100/200GbE or InfiniBand.
- CUDA + NCCL stack available on Dedicated/Private.
- Model families: GPT-style causal transformers, up to 70B (sharded) and beyond for future work.
- Workloads: low-concurrency latency-sensitive chat (single token step-by-step) and high-throughput batched generation.

Design components:
1) Sharding strategies (high-level)
- Data-parallel (DP): replicate full weights, scale batch throughput. Simple but memory limited for very large models.
- Tensor-parallel (TP): shard weight matrices (e.g., column/row parallelism) to distribute compute and memory across GPUs per step. Good for single-stage parallelism when attention/feedforward are large.
- Pipeline-parallel (PP): split the transformer layers across GPUs, enabling model-parallel sequencing. Adds micro-batching and pipeline bubbles tradeoffs.
- Hybrid TP+PP: combine approaches to scale both depth and width.
Decision: runtime must support all three modes with a declarative config. Default for >16GB model per-GPU: prefer TP+PP hybrid with automatic placement heuristics.

2) Placement & topology heuristics
- Prefer intra-node grouping for TP ranks to exploit NVLink/NVSwitch. Assign PP stage boundaries aligned to NVLink domains where possible.
- For multi-node deployments, prefer mapping PP stage boundaries to node boundaries to reduce cross-node all-to-all during activation forwarding.
- Provide a placement planner that takes: model layer sizes, per-GPU memory, interconnect topology, and SLO hints (latency vs throughput), then outputs a rank map.
- Fast path: default small config that maps TP ranks within node and PP across nodes.

3) NCCL tuning and communication patterns
- Key patterns: all-reduce (optimizer-like, for DP), all-gather / reduce-scatter (TP weight/activation exchanges), point-to-point / sendrecv for PP activations, and all-to-all for certain fused kernels.
- Tuning knobs we expose: NCCL communicator splitting strategy, CUDA kernel launch priorities, stream assignment (separate comm vs compute streams), CUDA IPC usage for intra-node transfers, and NCCL algorithm hints (ring vs tree).
- Default: create separate NCCL communicators per pattern (tp_comm, pp_comm, kv_comm) to allow independent tuning. Use high-priority stream for comms that unblock critical path (single-step generation).
- On NVLink-heavy nodes, prefer NCCL ring with higher chunk sizes to reduce kernel launch overhead. On inter-node links, test tree-based algorithms for latency.
- Experimental: enable NCCL asynchronous rendezvous enabling overlap of comm and compute (non-blocking collectives) for token loop. Run benchmarks to select defaults per hardware class.

4) Kernel selection and fused ops
- Runtime will select kernels based on batch size, sequence length, and available parallelism. For TP, prefer fused matmul-GELU-bias kernels where available. For PP we coalesce small GPU ops to reduce kernel launch overhead.
- Implement batched attention kernels that can operate on split weights across TP ranks with local compute + reduce-scatter+all-gather steps.
- Prioritize minimizing per-token kernel launches for single-token generation (chat). Consider micro-batching strategy where we buffer a small amount (configurable) of concurrent requests to amortize kernel overhead without violating tail SLO.

5) KV-cache design across shards/stages
- KV-cache semantics: per-session persistent cache storing key/value tensors for previous tokens. Must be accessible by the rank executing attention for the current layer.
- Placement options:
  - Sharded per-rank: each TP/PP rank stores only the portion of KV relevant to its weight shards. Lowest memory and network load for local attention compute, requires local indexing.
  - Replicated per-stage: for PP stages with small per-rank memory, replicate the full KV at stage boundary to avoid cross-rank requests for keys. Simpler but memory-expensive.
  - Remote KV service: store KV in a fast shared memory or host-managed cache (RDMA or gRPC) and pull on demand. Tradeoffs: flexibility vs latency/Jitter.
- Default approach: sharded per-rank KV with optional per-stage replication for chat flows where latency is premium and memory allows. Provide a config to trade memory versus network.
- Consistency model: strong consistency for single-session pinned to a rank map. Re-sharding (e.g., during scaling or failover) must include a background migration protocol and a consistency barrier to avoid reading stale/missing KV.

6) Scheduling and runtime loop for online generation
- Token loop orchestration: pipeline stages and TP kernels must be orchestrated with a focus on minimizing critical path latency. Use event-driven scheduling with explicit comm/compute overlap.
- Prioritize single-request low-latency path: place comm streams and kernel launches so that the per-token reduce-scatter/all-gather is overlapped with local matmuls where possible.
- Background tasks: prefetching of KV (for upcoming layers), asynchronous micro-batch assembly, and opportunistic packing of small requests.
- Admission control: implement per-model queueing with priorities (interactive vs bulk). For interactive requests enforce small max batch size and prefetched KV pinned to expected ranks.

7) Fault tolerance and reconfiguration
- Node failure handling: small-scale checkpointing of KV-cache metadata for sessions to allow quick rebind to alternate rank map. On failure, briefly divert new requests to fallback smaller model variant or replicated ranks.
- Rolling reconfiguration: when scaling out/in, perform staged re-sharding with a migration window. During migration, both old and new owners may accept reads, with writes routed to both until cutover (2-phase commit-like).

Open questions / experiments to run:
- Best default TP split granularity for A100/H100 across families (e.g., 4-way vs 8-way). Benchmark memory, per-token latency, and network overhead.
- NCCL algorithm selection heuristics per topology: run a suite comparing ring/tree/alltoall algorithms across chunk sizes for common ops.
- KV replication vs on-demand fetch tradeoffs for session lengths (5-1000 tokens): simulate memory cost vs extra latency.
- Micro-batch sizing strategy for interactive flows: how many concurrent requests to wait for before executing kernels without violating 99.9th percentile SLO.
- Evaluate RDMA-backed remote KV store feasibility for Private deployments vs in-process sharded KV.

Migration & rollout plan (short):
- Phase 0: bench harness - implement reference TP and PP kernels in isolated test harness; run microbenchmarks to capture baseline.
- Phase 1: limited internal preview: enable multi-GPU serving on Dedicated clusters with small set of models + conservative defaults (intra-node TP, simple PP).
- Phase 2: hybrid sharding, NCCL tuning heuristics, KV replication option, expand to multi-node.
- Phase 3: expose advanced knobs in Optimize UI and API, enable auto-placement and migration.

Appendix: quick checklist for PRs and experiments
- Implement separate NCCL communicators and ensure they are created per-topology.
- Add high-priority CUDA streams for comms that are on the critical token path.
- KV metadata format: session_id, rank_map_version, per-rank-offsets (serialize as binary + JSON header in checkpointing).
- Add integration test: single-session streaming generation across N GPUs, assert per-token latency within 2x single-GPU baseline for short sequences.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Share this doc with SRE and private-deployments to validate interconnect assumptions.
- Create confluence page with placement planner API and sample rank maps.
- Wire up JIRA epics for the benchmarking suite.
- Schedule NCCL microbench run on Dedicated staging cluster next week.

This doc is iterative. Expect follow-ups with measured latency/throughput curves and concrete kernel selection table once microbenchmarks complete.

Unresolved: failover protocol details for session migration; exact serialization format for KV checkpoints; heuristics for auto-placement cost model.

End of draft.
